rv.q: In an occasionally cloudy play, she's giving a performance that burns through the roof—and reaches, as Ruth says, "beaucoup stars peekin through the vault of heavn."

Even so, Ruth and Magalee fight over signing the paper transferring the building to the developer. Two fine actors enact a very human tragedy told in the lovely local accent, the Louisiana patois, with quotidian references.
Erika Dickerson-Despenza's Katrina Cycle kicks off with a gorgeous production at the Public.
With this ambitious opening act, Dickerson-Despenza and the Public have set high expectations for a tale of biblical proportions.
This says two things to me – how expansive Dickerson-Despenza’s talent, and how Davis could explain why the Public Theater’s staging of “shadow/land” makes a difference...
In any case, playwrights with this kind of reach don't come along every day.

This time, however, the crucial concerns are not so adequately and outspokenly confronted that they raise Dickerson-Despenza’s follow-up Public piece nearly as high as the etched-in-memory Katrina waters rose.
The play becomes an island of hope and despair, of memory and of longing.

cn.t: Dickerson-Despenza's Katrina drama earns praise for its ambitious storytelling and strong performances, though some critics find it less gripping than her previous work. The production's blend of history, spirituality, and intimate family drama divides reviewers.
